questions.question: Which statement best characterizes a Markov decision process (MDP)?
questions.choice_A: A framework with states, actions, transition dynamics, and a reward function where the next-state distribution depends only on the current state and action
questions.choice_B: A framework where the reward depends on the entire history of states and actions, not just the current state
questions.choice_C: A deterministic optimization problem with no stochasticity in transitions or rewards
questions.choice_D: A learning setup where the agent only observes rewards but never states or actions

questions.question: In discounted return, what is the primary role of the discount factor $\gamma \in [0,1)$?
questions.choice_A: To scale rewards so that they sum to exactly 1 over time
questions.choice_B: To downweight future rewards, ensuring the infinite-horizon return is finite and emphasizing near-term outcomes
questions.choice_C: To normalize the reward distribution to have zero mean and unit variance
questions.choice_D: To encourage longer episodes by increasing the magnitude of future rewards

questions.question: What differentiates episodic tasks from continuing tasks in RL?
questions.choice_A: Episodic tasks assume deterministic transitions; continuing tasks assume stochastic transitions
questions.choice_B: Episodic tasks use average reward; continuing tasks cannot define an average reward
questions.choice_C: Episodic tasks terminate after a sequence of steps and often use returns per episode, while continuing tasks have no terminal state and often use discounted or average reward formulations
questions.choice_D: There is no practical difference; both are treated identically in modern RL

questions.question: Why are stochastic policies commonly used in policy gradient methods?
questions.choice_A: Because deterministic policies cannot represent optimal behavior in any MDP
questions.choice_B: Because stochastic policies remove the need for gradient estimation
questions.choice_C: Because stochastic policies are easier to evaluate off-policy
questions.choice_D: Because they enable exploration by sampling actions and admit low-variance score-function gradients via $\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a\mid s)$

questions.question: Which expression best captures the policy gradient theorem for a differentiable stochastic policy $\pi_\theta$?
questions.choice_A: $\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{s \sim d^{\pi}, a \sim \pi_\theta}[\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a\mid s) \, Q^{\pi}(s,a)]$
questions.choice_B: $\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}[\nabla_\theta Q^{\pi}(s,a)]$
questions.choice_C: $\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}[\nabla_\theta r(s,a)]$
questions.choice_D: $\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \nabla_\theta \mathbb{E}[r_t]$ without dependence on the state distribution

questions.question: The REINFORCE algorithm provides an unbiased gradient estimator using which key idea?
questions.choice_A: Estimating $\nabla_\theta Q^{\pi}(s,a)$ directly via temporal-difference learning
questions.choice_B: Using the score function estimator: $\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a\mid s)$ multiplied by a return signal from the same trajectory
questions.choice_C: Replacing stochastic policies with deterministic policies to reduce variance
questions.choice_D: Approximating the gradient by finite differences in action space

questions.question: What is the effect of subtracting a baseline $b(s)$ from the return in policy gradient estimators?
questions.choice_A: It introduces bias but reduces variance
questions.choice_B: It increases both bias and variance
questions.choice_C: It leaves the estimator unbiased while potentially reducing variance, provided $b(s)$ does not depend on the action
questions.choice_D: It eliminates the need for sampling actions from the policy

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of advantage estimators, such as generalized advantage estimation (GAE)?
questions.choice_A: To replace value functions altogether with Monte Carlo returns
questions.choice_B: To guarantee unbiased gradients with zero variance
questions.choice_C: To compute a per-action learning rate for policy updates
questions.choice_D: To reduce variance relative to using raw returns by centering the signal around the baseline, with a controllable bias-variance trade-off

questions.question: Why add an entropy regularization term to the policy optimization objective?
questions.choice_A: To encourage exploration by preventing premature collapse to highly peaked action distributions
questions.choice_B: To guarantee monotonic policy improvement
questions.choice_C: To ensure the policy becomes deterministic as quickly as possible
questions.choice_D: To replace the reward signal with a purely information-theoretic objective

questions.question: KL divergence penalties are often added to policy objectives (e.g., in trust-region or proximal methods). What is their intended effect?
questions.choice_A: To make the policy invariant to reward scaling
questions.choice_B: To constrain the update so the new policy does not move too far from a reference policy, stabilizing learning
questions.choice_C: To force the policy to match the optimal Q-function exactly
questions.choice_D: To eliminate the need for baselines or advantage estimators

questions.question: How do the state-value function $V^{\pi}(s)$ and action-value function $Q^{\pi}(s,a)$ differ?
questions.choice_A: $V^{\pi}(s)$ averages over rewards of all policies; $Q^{\pi}(s,a)$ is policy-independent
questions.choice_B: $V^{\pi}(s)$ depends on the action taken; $Q^{\pi}(s,a)$ does not
questions.choice_C: $V^{\pi}(s)$ is the expected return from state $s$ following $\pi$, while $Q^{\pi}(s,a)$ is the expected return from state $s$ taking action $a$ then following $\pi$
questions.choice_D: They are identical by definition

questions.question: What distinguishes on-policy from off-policy policy gradient methods?
questions.choice_A: On-policy uses replay buffers; off-policy does not
questions.choice_B: On-policy learns a value function; off-policy cannot
questions.choice_C: On-policy uses importance sampling; off-policy does not
questions.choice_D: On-policy estimates gradients using data sampled from the current policy, whereas off-policy uses data from a different behavior policy and may require correction

questions.question: As $\gamma \to 1$ in an infinite-horizon continuing task with bounded rewards, what is a key consideration?
questions.choice_A: Variance of return estimates can grow and mixing properties of the Markov chain affect stability; average-reward formulations may become preferable
questions.choice_B: The policy gradient becomes zero regardless of the policy
questions.choice_C: The MDP becomes episodic by definition
questions.choice_D: Entropy regularization is no longer meaningful

questions.question: Why is the log-likelihood trick central to policy gradient methods?
questions.choice_A: It converts deterministic policies into stochastic ones
questions.choice_B: It rewrites $\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(a\mid s)$ as $\pi_\theta(a\mid s) \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a\mid s)$, allowing gradients to pass through sampling via expectations
questions.choice_C: It removes the need for value function approximation
questions.choice_D: It ensures unbiasedness even with action-dependent baselines

questions.question: Which practice respects the causality principle in REINFORCE-style estimators?
questions.choice_A: Weighting the gradient at time $t$ by the sum of all rewards in the episode
questions.choice_B: Weighting the gradient at time $t$ by only past rewards
questions.choice_C: Weighting the gradient at time $t$ by the return from time $t$ onward, excluding rewards before $t$
questions.choice_D: Weighting the gradient at time $t$ by a constant baseline that can depend on future states

questions.question: Why must a baseline used in policy gradient updates not depend on the action?
questions.choice_A: Because action-dependent baselines increase variance but remain unbiased
questions.choice_B: Because action-dependent baselines make the estimator biased only for continuous actions
questions.choice_C: Because baselines should be global constants to ensure stability
questions.choice_D: Because an action-dependent baseline alters the expected gradient and introduces bias unless carefully corrected

questions.question: What are common sources of variance in REINFORCE, and which approach helps mitigate them?
questions.choice_A: Stochastic transitions and high return variance; using state-dependent baselines and advantage normalization can reduce variance
questions.choice_B: Function approximation error; using a lower learning rate eliminates variance
questions.choice_C: Deterministic dynamics; adding noise to the environment reduces variance
questions.choice_D: Short episodes; truncating returns earlier increases estimator accuracy

questions.question: How does the entropy temperature (weight) affect learning when added to the objective?
questions.choice_A: Higher temperature always improves final performance
questions.choice_B: Higher temperature encourages more stochastic policies (more exploration) but can slow convergence; too low can cause premature collapse
questions.choice_C: Temperature only affects discrete action spaces
questions.choice_D: Temperature determines the episode length directly

questions.question: What important property of KL divergence matters when using KL penalties or constraints in policy optimization?
questions.choice_A: KL is symmetric, so the direction does not matter
questions.choice_B: KL equals squared Euclidean distance for small policy changes
questions.choice_C: KL is asymmetric; using $\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{\text{old}} \parallel \pi_{\text{new}})$ versus $\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{\text{new}} \parallel \pi_{\text{old}})$ can induce different behaviors (e.g., mode-covering vs. mode-seeking)
questions.choice_D: KL divergence is undefined for continuous action spaces

questions.question: Why is it beneficial to normalize or standardize advantage estimates within a batch?
questions.choice_A: It ensures unbiasedness of the gradient estimator
questions.choice_B: It replaces the need for entropy regularization
questions.choice_C: It eliminates the need for a baseline
questions.choice_D: It improves numerical stability and can reduce variance by making gradient magnitudes more consistent across updates

questions.question: Which description best captures the high-level difference between using returns, advantages, and Q-values in policy gradient updates?
questions.choice_A: Returns provide low variance but high bias; Q-values are unbiased but high variance; advantages are always unbiased and zero variance
questions.choice_B: Returns use only immediate rewards; Q-values use only long-term rewards; advantages mix both
questions.choice_C: Returns can be high variance; Q-values aim to estimate action-conditional returns; advantages center the signal by subtracting a baseline to reduce variance while preserving the gradient direction
questions.choice_D: There is no practical difference; all three produce identical gradients
